Galois groups of Taylor polynomials: prescriptions and arithmetic families

KN

Khai-Hoan Nguyen-Dang

Published Oct 27, 2026Fresh — published within the last 30 days · v2 · 78 min read

AI contributions
  • OpenAI ChatGPT Astra
View details →

Abstract

Let fn(x)=∑j=0najxjf_n(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n a_jx^jfn​(x)=∑j=0n​aj​xj be the Taylor polynomials of a power series with nonzero rational coefficients. We study the proportions of degrees for which the Galois group over \Q is symmetric, alternating, or neither. We prove that the set of degrees n≥3n\geq3n≥3 with symmetric group can be chosen arbitrarily, even for an entire function with positive rational coefficients whose Taylor polynomials have distinct negative real roots. More precisely, at each degree n≥3n\geq3n≥3 outside the chosen set, fnf_nfn​ has exactly one rational root, and the group on the other roots is the full symmetric group. Thus the proportions need not converge; when they do, the proportion of other groups can be any number in [0,1][0,1][0,1]. These conclusions answer negatively two questions of Katz and Rivin. Moreover, for fixed s\in\Q\setminus\Z, we also give a condition on the prime divisors of rational multipliers of the coefficients s/(s+j)s/(s+j)s/(s+j) that forces symmetric groups in density one. For the Taylor polynomials of (1−x)−s(1-x)^{-s}(1−x)−s, we determine the groups in all sufficiently large degrees. The number of exceptions to the symmetric group up to degree XXX is csX+Os(1)c_s\sqrt X+O_s(1)cs​X​+Os​(1), with an explicit constant cs≥0c_s\geq0cs​≥0. We also determine the groups of the central-binomial Taylor polynomials in every degree and prove that every nonconstant Catalan Taylor polynomial has symmetric group. This proves Sun's Catalan group conjecture and his irreducible-reduction criterion for the monic reciprocals of the central-binomial polynomials.

Introduction

Let

f(x)=∑j≥0ajxj∈Q[[x]],aj≠0,fn(x)=∑j=0najxj.f(x)=\sum_{j\geq0}a_jx^j\in\mathbb{Q}[[x]],\qquad a_j\ne0,\qquad f_n(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n a_jx^j.f(x)=j≥0∑​aj​xj∈Q[[x]],aj​=0,fn​(x)=j=0∑n​aj​xj.

We study the Galois group over Q\mathbb{Q}Q of the degree-nnn Taylor polynomial fnf_nfn​ as nnn varies. In particular, we ask how often this group is the symmetric group Sn\mathfrak{S}_nSn​, the alternating group An\mathfrak{A}_nAn​, or neither.

The classical example is the exponential series. Schur proved in 1930 that

En(x)=∑j=0nxjj!,n≥1,E_n(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n\frac{x^j}{j!},\qquad n\geq1,En​(x)=j=0∑n​j!xj​,n≥1,

has Galois group An\mathfrak{A}_nAn​ when 4∣n4\mid n4∣n and Sn\mathfrak{S}_nSn​ otherwise [40]. Symmetric groups therefore occur in three quarters of the degrees and alternating groups in one quarter. Coleman’s proof [11] uses Newton polygons to obtain permutations in the Galois group from the prime divisibility of the factorial denominators. Related arguments apply to generalized Laguerre polynomials [21].

On the other hand, the geometric series gives a different example. Its Taylor polynomial is (xn+1−1)/(x−1)(x^{n+1}-1)/(x-1)(xn+1−1)/(x−1), so its splitting field is cyclotomic and its group is abelian. For n≥4n\geq4n≥4 the group is therefore neither Sn\mathfrak{S}_nSn​ nor An\mathfrak{A}_nAn​. In these two examples, all three proportions converge, and the proportion of groups of neither kind is zero or one.

Katz and Rivin [26 Questions 1.1–1.2] ask whether this happens for every power series with nonzero rational coefficients. More precisely, they ask whether the three proportions always converge and, when they all converge, whether the third limit must be zero or one.

Our first result answers both questions negatively. We prove that for any set of degrees B⊆{3,4,…}B \subseteq\{3,4,\ldots\}B⊆{3,4,…}, we construct an entire function with positive rational coefficients such that, for n≥3n \ge3n≥3, its degree-nnn Taylor polynomial has group Sn\mathcal{S}_nSn​ precisely when n∈Bn \in Bn∈B. In the remaining degrees n≥3n \ge3n≥3, it has one rational root and an irreducible factor of degree n−1n-1n−1 with group Sn−1\mathcal{S}_{n-1}Sn−1​. Every Taylor polynomial has distinct negative real roots. Thus even these restrictions on convergence, signs, and zeros leave the set of symmetric degrees arbitrary.

We then give conditions on the prime divisors of the coefficients that force the symmetric group to occur in density one. For nonintegral binomial powers, an exact discriminant formula determines the exceptional degrees and gives their asymptotic number. For the central-binomial and Catalan generating functions, we determine the groups in every degree over Q\mathbb{Q}Q.

The same frequency conclusions hold over every number field, since only finitely many of these segment groups can change after extending the ground field (Corollary 7.7).

An arithmetic condition for density one

We next consider polynomials obtained from ∑j=0ssxj/(s+j)\sum_{j=0}^{s} sx^j/(s+j)∑j=0s​sxj/(s+j), with fixed s∈Q∖Zs\in\mathbb{Q}\setminus\mathbb{Z}s∈Q∖Z, by multiplying each coefficient by a nonzero rational number. We impose a condition on the prime factors of these multipliers: their numerators and denominators, in lowest terms, have no prime factor larger than n+Cn+Cn+C, where C≥0C\geq0C≥0 is fixed. The condition preserves the coefficient valuations at primes larger than n+Cn+Cn+C, which are the primes used in the proof.

We state the result over a number field FFF. Let RFR_FRF​ be the largest rational prime ramified in FFF, with RQ=1R_{\mathbb{Q}}=1RQ​=1. The explicit integer N(a,b,C,F)N(a,b,C,F)N(a,b,C,F) is defined in (25). For frequencies over FFF, we use the notation sf,F(N),af,F(N),of,F(N)s_{f,F}(N),a_{f,F}(N),o_{f,F}(N)sf,F​(N),af,F​(N),of,F​(N) and SF(f),AF(f),OF(f)S_F(f),A_F(f),O_F(f)SF​(f),AF​(f),OF​(f), obtained by replacing Q\mathbb{Q}Q with FFF in the definitions above.
